This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
In 2014, residents and environmental groups argued in a lawsuit that a California Department of Transportation road project planned to run through Richardson Grove State Park failed to properly evaluate how it could harm the redwood trees. It still took courts a total of 15 years to resolve all of the related legal complaints before Caltrans could move forward with building.
Environmental advocates say the litigation led to changes that better protect redwood trees. But pro-building advocates point to the case as evidence that the California Environmental Quality Act and the review process it requires need an overhaul.
Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) , a November ballot initiative that aims to streamline the process, would change how fights like this one play out.
At the heart of the debate over the measure is who holds power over environmental reviews. Some legal experts say Prop. 45 would shift power away from courts and the public, giving project applicants, who include developers and public agencies building their own projects, more control at key points. For public agencies, including cities, counties and state entities, it’s complicated: an agency could lose discretion when it reviews someone else’s project and gain speed and certainty when it builds its own.
The California Chamber of Commerce, the measure’s sponsor, says the measure would cut costs by speeding up building. Critics say it goes much further than streamlining.
“This is not surgical at all,” said Ethan Elkind, a climate law expert at the Berkeley School of Law. “This would be a sea change.”
How does CEQA work?
California’s landmark environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to take into account the environmental impacts of a development and help avoid them.
Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down needed housing. Environmental groups say it gives communities a say in how projects get built.
In response to a housing shortage and high prices, state leaders have moved to ease CEQA’s reach over housing. Most recently, in 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) projects from having to go through a lengthy environmental review process.
Prop. 45 would reach housing that doesn’t qualify for those exemptions, along with roads, water and other infrastructure projects.
Contractors with PG&E work in a trench to lay underground electric cables in Placer County on Oct. 17, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters Under the current process, public agencies are responsible for reviewing the potential environmental impacts of projects. Project applicants, usually developers, present an initial study summarizing the expected impacts. The lead public agency overseeing the review decides whether the impacts are significant enough to warrant more thorough scrutiny.
Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, , and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

Prop 45 explained: CEQA overhaul could shift who holds power over building
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)
October 9, 2026 5:00 am

This story was originally published by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/). Sign up (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/) for their newsletters.
In 2014, residents and environmental groups argued in a lawsuit that a California Department of Transportation road project planned to run through Richardson Grove State Park failed to properly evaluate how it could harm the redwood trees. It still took courts a total of 15 years to resolve all of the related legal complaints before Caltrans could move forward with building.
Environmental advocates say the litigation led to changes that better protect redwood trees. But pro-building advocates point to the case as evidence that the California Environmental Quality Act and the review process it requires need an overhaul.
Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) , a November ballot initiative that aims to streamline the process, would change how fights like this one play out.
At the heart of the debate over the measure is who holds power over environmental reviews. Some legal experts say Prop. 45 would shift power away from courts and the public, giving project applicants, who include developers and public agencies building their own projects, more control at key points. For public agencies, including cities, counties and state entities, it’s complicated: an agency could lose discretion when it reviews someone else’s project and gain speed and certainty when it builds its own.
The California Chamber of Commerce, the measure’s sponsor, says the measure would cut costs by speeding up building. Critics say it goes much further than streamlining.
“This is not surgical at all,” said Ethan Elkind, a climate law expert at the Berkeley School of Law. “This would be a sea change.”
How does CEQA work?
California’s landmark environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to take into account the environmental impacts of a development and help avoid them.
Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down needed housing. Environmental groups say it gives communities a say in how projects get built.
In response to a housing shortage and high prices, state leaders have moved to ease CEQA’s reach over housing. Most recently, in 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) projects from having to go through a lengthy environmental review process.
Prop. 45 would reach housing that doesn’t qualify for those exemptions, along with roads, water and other infrastructure projects.
Contractors with PG&E work in a trench to lay underground electric cables in Placer County on Oct. 17, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters Under the current process, public agencies are responsible for reviewing the potential environmental impacts of projects. Project applicants, usually developers, present an initial study summarizing the expected impacts. The lead public agency overseeing the review decides whether the impacts are significant enough to warrant more thorough scrutiny.
Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, , and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

Let me also think about what matters most. Key facts I've gathered:

**What Prop 45 does:**
- Sponsored by Cal Chamber, qualified via signatures
- Creates an optional expedited CEQA process for 8-9 categories of "essential" projects: housing, water (except Delta tunnel), clean energy (except nuclear), healthcare, public safety, wildfire mitigation, broadband, education, transportation (except high-speed rail)
- Enforceable deadlines: 30 days to deem application complete (one corrections list), 365 days to certify EIR, 90 days for permits, hearings within 60 days if deadlines missed
- Courts must resolve suits in 270 days (+90 extension)
- Applicant develops only one project alternative (instead of agency considering multiple)
- Review based on laws/standards in place at application submission
- Limits public comment periods to a max, restricts what comments go into the record
- Tribal consultation limited to federally recognized tribes
- Courts can't stop the whole project, only the non-compliant portion; once a court signs off, no further lawsuits
- Fiscal: initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; long-term uncertain, could be positive or negative

**Supporters:** Cal Chamber, CA GOP, hospital associations, water association, affordable housing council, building industry, some clean energy groups, NAACP CA, LULAC, CalTax, farm bureau. Editorials: SD U-T, OC Register, Sac Bee/McClatchy, Mercury News. Funded ~$56M by utilities, developers, tech (Brin, Doerr $10M), oil (California Resources Corp $1M+).

**Opponents:** CA Democratic Party, Sierra Club CA, environmental voters, nurses, labor federation, League of Women Voters, Western Center on Law & Poverty, 550+ coalition. SF Chronicle editorial "no". NYT critical. Funded ~$30M including Wendy Schmidt $10M.

**Key criticisms:**
- Goes too far: could fast-track polluting projects, data centers, warehouses, sprawl development, freeway expansion
- Limits public input, narrows judicial review
- Applies same streamlining to infill housing and freeway/sprawl projects
- Drafted by and funded by corporate interests; poll-tested exclusions (HSR, delta tunnel)
- Uncertainty: litigation over ambiguous provisions (data centers)
- Locks complex policy into statute via initiative, hard to fix
- Alternatives: Legislature has been passing CEQA reforms (SB 743, AB 1307, infill exemptions, SB 205... etc.)
- Expert CEQA reformers split: some support, many neutral or oppose; Tom Steyer opposes; SPUR declined to support; Newsom hasn't taken a position

**Key arguments for:**
- CEQA is widely abused; delays add huge costs; housing crisis; NIMBY weaponization
- Study: 78% of CEQA litigation disproportionately challenges housing in higher-income neighborhoods (that's a pro-reform data point)
- Most projects covered are objectively beneficial (housing, hospitals, wildfire mitigation, clean energy)
- Still requires full EIR and compliance with all other environmental laws (Clean Air Act, Clean Water Act, ESA etc.)
- Local control retained
- Deadlines only make existing nominal deadlines enforceable

That’s what Californians need to answer before voting on Proposition 45 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-45-ceqa-housing-data-center-voter-guide), which would substantially change the state’s landmark environmental protection law.
The business-backed ballot measure would make it much easier and less costly to build loads of projects — not just housing, but also water works, clean energy and transportation facilities.
It also, however, would give citizens much less time and fewer tools to assess and oppose projects they deem unfit for their area — such as freeway expansions or giant warehouses.

“It tips the scale from favoring the public and the environment to favoring developers and polluting projects,” asserts state Sen. Catherine Blakespear (D-Encinitas), chair of the Senate Environmental Quality Committee.

“We streamline the building process for billionaires to erect stadiums. Why don’t we do it for middle-class homebuyers?” declares Dan Dunmoyer, president and chief executive of the California Building Industry Assn., a major backer of Proposition 45.
It’s a bitter, high-stakes fight that’s too close to call. Polling has indicated the outcome could be decided in the final days before the Nov. 3 election.

Proposition 45 would be the most significant overhaul of the California Environmental Quality Act since Republican Gov. Ronald Reagan signed it in 1970.
CEQA — as it’s commonly called and used as a four-letter obscenity by developers — is justifiably credited with keeping California air less polluted, water relatively clean, urban traffic from being worse and more outdoors open to the public.
It requires developers — private and public — to undergo a lengthy process of analyzing a project’s environmental effects and reducing their negative impacts.
But over the years CEQA became blatantly abused.
Union blackmailers — ”greenmailers” — threatened frivolous CEQA lawsuits unless developers caved to labor demands. Business rivals drove off potential competitors by filing protracted suits that wore down investors. NIMBYs — ”not in my backyard” — fought local projects that crowded their spaces or blocked views.
As a CEQA battle dragged on, the developers’ costs soared and many cut their losses by abandoning the project. Home building plummeted in California and the law of supply and demand ruled. Housing costs skyrocketed.
Project opponents legitimately concerned about environmental impacts also filed lawsuits, but they weren’t the developer’s big problem — not like the CEQA abusers.

Gavin Newsom, lawmakers have been responding in recent years (https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-sac-stadium-bills-failures-20170411-story.html)to the developers’ frustration. They’ve been pecking away at CEQA (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-07-01/environmental-groups-outraged-by-newsom-overhaul-ceqa) with meaningful reforms for most types of housing, especially urban apartment projects near transit hubs.
“You’ve got to just move things,” Newsom exclaimed at an economic summit in Long Beach last week. “I’m just done with the [CEQA] litigation…. Years and years of B.S…. Eight years to develop something? Give me a break.”
But the nearly termed-out governor still hadn’t taken a position on Proposition 45.
Money and power, of course, have always had their privileges in the state Capitol. Billionaire sports team owners have had no trouble securing CEQA exemptions for construction of new stadiums or arenas. The exemptions are handed out like free bobbleheads.

“It doesn’t help the first-time middle-class homebuyers or address market rate rentals.”
He pegs the cost of a CEQA battle at $75,000 per new home, noting that’s added to the selling price — if the dwelling ever gets built.

And that led to longer smog-spewing car commutes to city jobs.
“Sprawl housing is not affordable housing,” Blakespear says. “There are costs to build new infrastructure like utility lines and water facilities, and high insurance costs. Then taxpayers have to clean up the pollution.
“Do we really want new sprawl housing developments in wildfire areas? We need to incentivize [urban] infill housing, instead of in the middle of the forest or the desert.”

Prop 45 explained: CEQA overhaul could shift who holds power over building
by
CalMatters (https://www.almanacnews.com/author/calmatters/)

In 2014, residents and environmental groups argued in a lawsuit that a California Department of Transportation road project planned to run through Richardson Grove State Park failed to properly evaluate how it could harm the redwood trees. It still took courts a total of 15 years to resolve all of the related legal complaints before Caltrans could move forward with building.
Environmental advocates say the litigation led to changes that better protect redwood trees. But pro-building advocates point to the case as evidence that the California Environmental Quality Act and the review process it requires need an overhaul.
Proposition 45 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/) , a November ballot initiative that aims to streamline the process, would change how fights like this one play out.
At the heart of the debate over the measure is who holds power over environmental reviews. Some legal experts say Prop. 45 would shift power away from courts and the public, giving project applicants, who include developers and public agencies building their own projects, more control at key points. For public agencies, including cities, counties and state entities, it’s complicated: an agency could lose discretion when it reviews someone else’s project and gain speed and certainty when it builds its own.
The California Chamber of Commerce, the measure’s sponsor, says the measure would cut costs by speeding up building. Critics say it goes much further than streamlining.
“This is not surgical at all,” said Ethan Elkind, a climate law expert at the Berkeley School of Law. “This would be a sea change.”
How does CEQA work?
California’s landmark environmental review law, signed in 1970, requires agencies to take into account the environmental impacts of a development and help avoid them.
Over decades, developers have raised concerns about the process, arguing litigation and bureaucracy slow down needed housing. Environmental groups say it gives communities a say in how projects get built.
In response to a housing shortage and high prices, state leaders have moved to ease CEQA’s reach over housing. Most recently, in 2025, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed laws that exempt many housing (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) projects from having to go through a lengthy environmental review process.
Prop. 45 would reach housing that doesn’t qualify for those exemptions, along with roads, water and other infrastructure projects.
Contractors with PG&E work in a trench to lay underground electric cables in Placer County on Oct. 17, 2024. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters Under the current process, public agencies are responsible for reviewing the potential environmental impacts of projects. Project applicants, usually developers, present an initial study summarizing the expected impacts. The lead public agency overseeing the review decides whether the impacts are significant enough to warrant more thorough scrutiny.
Public agencies are responsible for comparing the effects of a range of project alternatives, including a “no project” scenario.
Agencies judge project impacts using environmental standards they choose, covering everything from noise to air pollution, and they can revise those standards as new information emerges.
The public can then submit comments and suggest project alternatives, which the lead agency must consider. Members of the public, environmental groups and other stakeholders can sue to challenge reviews they think are illegal or incomplete.
Prop. 45 would give agencies 365 business days to decide on an environmental impact report for projects the measure defines as essential, including housing, roads, water, broadband and wildfire mitigation, , and require courts to resolve cases within 270 calendar days.
Eligible applicants could choose the new procedures or stay with the existing ones.
What supporters and opponents say
Supporters of Prop. 45 say that the current process causes unnecessary delays and expenses, (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) including the costs of reviewing late public comments and defending against litigation.
Jennifer Barrera, chief executive of the California Chamber of Commerce, said the delays are costly.
“Time is money, and the delays that we see with regards to all of the red tape and bureaucracy … it could be anywhere from six to 10 years added on to the determination of moving a project forward,” Barrera said. “All those costs are ultimately borne by the consumers.”
Dan Dunmoyer, chief executive of the California Building Industry Association, said the proposition would decrease the cost of the average home by $75,000.
“If we want to have a society where people can live and thrive, we’ve got to find the sweet spot, and we think Prop. 45 is the sweet spot,” Dunmoyer said.
Opponents — a coalition that includes environmental groups, some labor unions and the California Democratic Party — say the measure goes far beyond basic streamlining, and gives project applicants too much power, undercutting the point of CEQA. They say Prop. 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate agencies’ ability to enforce the law.
“When you’re undoing or undermining environmental review, or saying you don’t need to do as much environmental review, you can have less community input for a project,” said Aruna Prabhala, an attorney for the Center for Biological Diversity who works on the opposition campaign.
A power shift?
Prop. 45 doesn’t just make the process go faster. It also changes (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) the rules for project applicants and the government agencies overseeing the review process, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office, the Legislature’s nonpartisan adviser.
Applicants could choose just one project alternative for the agency to consider rather than the multiple alternatives agencies assess today. Agencies would have to judge a project’s impacts under the standards in place when the applicant applies, rather than revising them as new information emerges, and list everything an application requires up front. If an agency misses the 365-business-day deadline, the applicant could request a hearing and potentially sue.
The public and courts would have less say. Public comments would be subject to a strict 45-day deadline, and any late comments can’t be entered into the record that a judge could review if there’s litigation.
Courts could still order agencies to fix flawed reviews, but could stop only the part of a project that failed to comply, not the whole project.
The same rules would apply when public agencies are developers themselves. Agencies building roads or water systems, for instance, would have the option of just analyzing one project alternative and choosing the environmental rules that apply at the time of submission. If they’re sued and a court finds they made a mistake with just one piece of their review, the overall project could still move forward.
Sean Marciniak, an attorney for Hanson Bridgett, which helped the California Chamber of Commerce write the measure, said agencies would keep the power to reject projects and the measure would not override other planning or zoning laws.
“This will protect agencies in their decisions,” he said.
Why a county group is sitting this out
Organizations that represent local governments in California, including the League of California Cities and the California State Association of Counties, have mostly stayed out of the debate.
California’s rural counties say they have a problem with building housing, and they’ve historically advocated for CEQA reform.
These counties often have small populations. They’re strapped for cash and the staff needed to handle the complicated process, said John Kennedy, a policy advocate for the Rural County Representatives of California.
So when the California Chamber of Commerce proposed a ballot initiative to speed up environmental reviews, Prop. 45 at first looked like a natural fit.
“CEQA has long been misused and manipulated by a number of interest groups seeking to extract their own interests,” Kennedy said.
But the group, which represents parts of 40 counties, is sitting this one out. Its leaders voted to stay neutral; Kennedy said he suggested the group oppose it because he thinks it goes too far.
“Prop. 45 really puts the power in the hands of the project proponents, project developers, and limits local authority to require consideration of alternatives,” he said.
He worries local agencies would lose control over the standards that decide when noise, dust or runoff is significant enough to require action.
What Prop. 45 would have changed
In Richardson Grove, had the Caltrans case come up after Prop. 45, Caltrans could have benefited from a 270-calendar-day time limit on courts to resolve the case. If a court found a flaw, it could stop only the part of the project that fell short.
The case, Marciniak said, also shows how Caltrans could have used existing standards to make the review go more smoothly and quickly. In 2014, an appeals court found Caltrans’ environmental report applied no standard for judging harm to the redwoods’ roots, and noted a state parks handbook with guidelines for protecting trees from construction damage. “There are easy tweaks any agency can make to crystallize meaningful thresholds of significance,” he said.
Opponents say the case is not typical. It’s rare for a case to take so long, said Doug Carstens, an attorney who often represents environmental groups in CEQA cases. The fixes courts required made the review better, he added.
“In this instance you’re talking about trees, but Prop. 45 could also apply to an instance where there’s people,” Carstens said. “It’s a question of going too far.”
What would it cost, and what would it save
New housing construction in the Crocker Village neighborhood in Sacramento on Feb. 10, 2022. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters The measure’s backers pitch it as an answer to California’s cost-of-living crisis.
Amelia Matier, a spokesperson for the Prop. 45 campaign, said faster, more predictable reviews would let California build housing and infrastructure at lower cost.
A study by Blue Sky Consulting Group, commissioned by the California Chamber of Commerce, estimates state and local governments and other public agencies would see $1.5 billion in combined savings and additional revenues.
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that state and local governments and courts would face initial costs in the high tens of millions of dollars annually, potentially more than $100 million, over the first several years, partly covered by fees.
Some costs would likely decline over time, the office said, but long-term impacts are unclear. For instance, faster building would likely lower project costs, but any harmful environmental impacts resulting from quicker reviews would cost state and local agencies more.
Carstens said the savings aren’t even guaranteed, and that the Chamber of Commerce is using the affordability debate to deregulate in favor of business.
“They say it’s about affordable housing, but that’s not anywhere visible in this measure,” Carstens said. “There’s no affordability provision or requirement for addressing the needs of people who are impoverished and underprivileged.”
If Prop. 45 passes, much would be left to the courts. The measure says it should be interpreted to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving and building essential projects. Opponents say that would tilt unclear language in favor of applicants.
Marciniak said the provision is meant for situations the authors couldn’t predict.
“There is going to be confusion, but I think importantly, a judge in California is going to look at this and understand immediately what it means,” he said.

Ideas expressed in the piece
The column argues that CEQA has helped protect California’s air, water and open space, but acknowledges that frivolous lawsuits, labor pressure and local opposition have sometimes delayed or killed projects and contributed to higher housing costs.
However, it contends that Proposition 45 goes too far: by shortening environmental reviews and legal challenges for a broad range of projects, the measure would leave communities less time and fewer tools to identify and contest harmful impacts. The measure would also limit aspects of agency review, public comment and court oversight, according to the UC Berkeley guide. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45)
The article warns that broad streamlining could encourage sprawl, with added infrastructure costs, longer car commutes and development in wildfire-prone areas. It argues that lawmakers have already made significant CEQA changes for some housing, and that further reforms should be worked out through the Legislature rather than a ballot measure that would be difficult to amend. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45) [4] (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/)
While the column does not accept opponents’ claim that data centers are clearly covered by the measure, it says the proposal could facilitate other undesirable projects. Other coverage describes the eligibility of broadband projects as a point of dispute, with opponents warning that it could extend streamlined review to data centers. [2] (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2026-10-14/californias-prop-45-aims-to-speed-construction-projects-opponents-say-data-centers-will-benefit) [7] (https://www.bisnow.com/news/los-angeles/commercial-real-estate/california-election-proposition-45-ceqa)
Different views on the topic
Supporters argue that CEQA reviews and lawsuits can make needed housing and infrastructure slow and costly to build. They say Proposition 45’s deadlines for reviews and court challenges would reduce delays and costs for homes, water systems, clean-energy projects, transportation and other facilities, with savings benefiting consumers and taxpayers. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45) [4] (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/)
Backers also contend that the proposal streamlines the process rather than removing environmental laws: eligible projects would remain subject to environmental standards and local approval, while agencies would face clearer timelines. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45) [6] (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22444826.php)
The California Building Industry Assn. argues that existing reforms are too limited in scope—particularly for housing beyond urban infill and transit areas—and that faster approvals are needed to address the state’s broader housing shortage, including market-rate rentals and homes for middle-income buyers. [3] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-45-ceqa-housing-data-center-voter-guide) [5] (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/16/endorsement-proposition-45-november3-ballot-initiative-ceqa-reform-housing-costs/)

Ideas expressed in the piece
The column argues that CEQA has helped protect California’s air, water and open space, but acknowledges that frivolous lawsuits, labor pressure and local opposition have sometimes delayed or killed projects and contributed to higher housing costs.
However, it contends that Proposition 45 goes too far: by shortening environmental reviews and legal challenges for a broad range of projects, the measure would leave communities less time and fewer tools to identify and contest harmful impacts. The measure would also limit aspects of agency review, public comment and court oversight, according to the UC Berkeley guide. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45)
The article warns that broad streamlining could encourage sprawl, with added infrastructure costs, longer car commutes and development in wildfire-prone areas. It argues that lawmakers have already made significant CEQA changes for some housing, and that further reforms should be worked out through the Legislature rather than a ballot measure that would be difficult to amend. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45) [4] (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/)
While the column does not accept opponents’ claim that data centers are clearly covered by the measure, it says the proposal could facilitate other undesirable projects. Other coverage describes the eligibility of broadband projects as a point of dispute, with opponents warning that it could extend streamlined review to data centers. [2] (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2026-10-14/californias-prop-45-aims-to-speed-construction-projects-opponents-say-data-centers-will-benefit) [7] (https://www.bisnow.com/news/los-angeles/commercial-real-estate/california-election-proposition-45-ceqa)
Different views on the topic
Supporters argue that CEQA reviews and lawsuits can make needed housing and infrastructure slow and costly to build. They say Proposition 45’s deadlines for reviews and court challenges would reduce delays and costs for homes, water systems, clean-energy projects, transportation and other facilities, with savings benefiting consumers and taxpayers. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45) [4] (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-45-environmental-review/)
Backers also contend that the proposal streamlines the process rather than removing environmental laws: eligible projects would remain subject to environmental standards and local approval, while agencies would face clearer timelines. [1] (https://igs.berkeley.edu/library/california-ballot-proposition-guides/november-3-2026-general-election/proposition-45) [6] (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/prop-45-ceqa-california-22444826.php)
The California Building Industry Assn. argues that existing reforms are too limited in scope—particularly for housing beyond urban infill and transit areas—and that faster approvals are needed to address the state’s broader housing shortage, including market-rate rentals and homes for middle-income buyers. [3] (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-45-ceqa-housing-data-center-voter-guide) [5] (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/16/endorsement-proposition-45-november3-ballot-initiative-ceqa-reform-housing-costs/)

The NYT article is paywalled (403). I have plenty of material. Let me do a couple more checks:

1. Polling on Prop 45 (PPIC September polling showed split)
2. The Yes campaign's response on data centers and sprawl — maybe check yesonprop45.com briefly.
3. Maybe check the Inside Climate News piece for the money angle (already have summary from search).

Let me also think about whether there's an official LA Times editorial board position on Prop 45. The CalMatters endorsement list only showed SF Chronicle on "oppose" and SD U-T, OC Register, Sac Bee, Mercury News on "support." The LA Times' editorial board stance — let me quickly search for that, plus PPIC polling.

Actually, the user asked "What should I vote on this prop?" with the constraint of answering yes or no. I've done substantial research: official voter guide (title/summary, LAO analysis, arguments/rebuttals), CalMatters explainer, SF Chronicle (No), SD U-T (Yes), Sac Bee (Yes), LA Times Skelton column (leaning No), Inside Climate News (critical), NYT (critical on sprawl), plus funding info.

The LAO's fiscal note (high costs, uncertain benefits) doesn't scream clear win. The "too complex for ballot, can't be amended" argument is strong given 41 pages of dense environmental law. And the tribal consultation narrowing and the "fullest possible weight" interpretive canon are red flags.

Also notable: the Chronicle — a paper that has repeatedly editorialized for CEQA reform and against NIMBY abuse — concluded "vote no" because the measure as written "would lock California into a regulatory regime that makes it easier to build the same environmentally ruinous projects that gave us CEQA in the first place." That's a persuasive signal from a source sympathetic to the reform goal.

Meanwhile, the strongest "yes" endorsements (SD U-T, Sac Bee, Mercury News, OC Register) are real, but their arguments mostly mirror the campaign's talking points and tend to underweight the drafting flaws (sprawl, ambiguity, un-amendability, tribal consultation).

I think the wiser, more defensible recommendation is NO — CEQA needs reform, but this particular measure goes too far in the wrong places, is too broad, locks in flawed policy, and its biggest beneficiaries are the corporate funders (utilities, oil, developers, tech data centers) while the fiscal costs are real and the affordability benefits are speculative (no affordability requirements in the measure).

Wait — but let me steelman the Yes once more. "Time is money" — six to 10 years of delay is genuinely ruinous; a 365-day enforceable EIR deadline is what other states effectively have; housing studies show CEQA litigation disproportionately targets housing (78% challenging housing in higher-income neighborhoods — i.e., NIMBYs weaponizing it). If we wait for the Legislature, we wait forever. The new governor and Legislature just passed major reform in 2025 though — so the "Legislature will never act" premise is weakening. And Prop 45's sprawl provisions might undo the climate/affordability benefits by subsidizing car-dependent fringe growth.

Also note: opponents include the California Democratic Party, League of Women Voters, labor, environmental justice groups; supporters include CA GOP, Chamber, developers. That alignment suggests the measure is more a partisan/corporate play than a technocratic fix — though there are cross-party figures on both sides (NAACP/LULAC support; some Republican county committees oppose).

Given everything, I'll recommend NO. The decisive factors:
1. Initiative statute essentially un-amendable (2/3 vote) — bad vehicle for 41 pages of intricate procedural law with predictable drafting flaws.
2. Drafting flaws with real-world consequences: sprawl/fast-tracking freeways, possible data centers, weakened tribal consultation, frozen standards, single applicant-drafted alternative, restricted public comment and judicial record, no whole-project injunctions, one-shot litigation.
3. LAO fiscal: initial costs up to $100M+/year, long-term effects uncertain (could be negative).
4. The best-projected benefits (housing affordability) are speculative — no affordability mandates; the marginal projects it uniquely speeds are precisely the ones CEQA exists to scrutinize (peripheral sprawl, freeways, industrial).
5. The Legislature has demonstrated recent capacity for targeted CEQA reform and is the right venue.
6. Endorsement signal: even reform-friendly institutions (SF Chronicle editorial board, SPUR, Steyer) decline to support or oppose; the coalition behind it is dominated by its corporate beneficiaries; oil money (CRC) is a notable funder.

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

Prop 45 Streamlines approvals to build essential projects faster and make California more affordable
Last updated: October 12, 2026
The Problem
California's cost of living is out of control. Our outdated system for approving housing, water projects, schools and hospitals (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) is too slow—and it's driving up the cost of living for all of us.
$75,000+ (https://yesonprop45.com/cost-of-delay-per-home/) added to every new home, which drives up rents and mortgages.
Billions added in taxpayer and consumer costs (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) for hospitals, roads and clean energy projects.
Delayed progress on critical environmental projects to reduce pollution, prevent wildfires (https://www.latimes.com/environment/story/2025-11-25/cal-fire-approach-to-socals-wildfire-crisis-could-make-things-worse-court-says) and cut emissions.
See real California projects delayed for years (https://yesonprop45.com/case-studies/) →
The Solution
Prop 45 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) cuts red tape and unnecessary delays so California can build the essential infrastructure we need faster, lower our cost of living and improve our quality of life.
Including:
Clean water infrastructure
Clean Energy
Housing
Roads, bridges, and transit
Hospitals and health care facilities
Schools and educational facilities
Wildfire prevention
Broadband infrastructure
What Is Prop 45?
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm), the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/), is a 2026 California ballot proposition that modernizes the state's outdated approval process for essential projects like housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools and hospitals by setting enforceable timelines (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) for agency decisions and court challenges, while keeping California's environmental, worker and tribal protections and local control (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) in place.

Prop 45 will:
Reduce the cost of living
An analysis by the Blue Sky Consulting Group estimates Prop 45 would add nearly 20,000 homes a year (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/), or nearly 200,000 over ten years.
Accelerate the essential infrastructure California needs
Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), and courts must resolve legal challenges within 270 days (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm).
Protect taxpayers by keeping public projects on time and on budget
The same analysis estimates $386 million a year in savings for public agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) on essential projects and $250 million a year for California ratepayers.
Create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy
Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California's strongest-in-the-nation labor standards (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Labor-Protections-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), including fair pay and safe job sites.
Protect local control and community input
Local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects, and Prop 45 guarantees a 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments.
Protect California's strong environmental, worker and tribal cultural protections
Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45); CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place.
Prop 45 speeds up approvals for the projects Californians rely on most:
Clean drinking water and supply projects
Hospitals, clinics and other health care facilities
Roads, bridges, transit and other transportation infrastructure
Wildfire prevention and resilience projects
Single and multi-family homes, senior and student housing
Clean energy generation, transmission and storage
Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
Schools, classrooms and educational facilities

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

California's cost of living is out of control. Our outdated system for approving housing, water projects, schools and hospitals (https://www.hklaw.com/-/media/files/insights/publications/2026/09/hernandez_2026ceqastudy.pdf) is too slow—and it's driving up the cost of living for all of us.

Prop 45 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) cuts red tape and unnecessary delays so California can build the essential infrastructure we need faster, lower our cost of living and improve our quality of life.
Including:
Clean water infrastructure
Clean Energy
Housing
Roads, bridges, and transit
Hospitals and health care facilities
Schools and educational facilities
Wildfire prevention
Broadband infrastructure
What Is Prop 45?
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm), the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/), is a 2026 California ballot proposition that modernizes the state's outdated approval process for essential projects like housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools and hospitals by setting enforceable timelines (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) for agency decisions and court challenges, while keeping California's environmental, worker and tribal protections and local control (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) in place.

Prop 45 will:
Reduce the cost of living
An analysis by the Blue Sky Consulting Group estimates Prop 45 would add nearly 20,000 homes a year (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/), or nearly 200,000 over ten years.
Accelerate the essential infrastructure California needs
Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), and courts must resolve legal challenges within 270 days (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm).
Protect taxpayers by keeping public projects on time and on budget
The same analysis estimates $386 million a year in savings for public agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) on essential projects and $250 million a year for California ratepayers.
Create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy
Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California's strongest-in-the-nation labor standards (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Labor-Protections-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), including fair pay and safe job sites.
Protect local control and community input
Local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects, and Prop 45 guarantees a 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments.
Protect California's strong environmental, worker and tribal cultural protections
Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45); CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place.
Prop 45 speeds up approvals for the projects Californians rely on most:
Clean drinking water and supply projects

Roads, bridges, transit and other transportation infrastructure
Wildfire prevention and resilience projects
Single and multi-family homes, senior and student housing
Clean energy generation, transmission and storage
Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
Schools, classrooms and educational facilities

Supporters say all substantive environmental laws remain; opponents say CEQA's procedural rigor is what makes those laws meaningful in practice.

The California Environmental Quality Act has been used in such an abusive way for more than 50 years that then-Gov. Jerry Brown’s 2012 description of CEQA reform as “the Lord’s work” has gone from being seen as a good one-liner from an unusually witty politician to a profound observation about life in the Golden State.
There is a reason the Legislature has had to pass so many CEQA exemptions:
Many major, valuable projects would never have been built without this protection. The 1970 state law makes it too easy for third parties to block or stall proposals that they don’t like or want to be paid to support. This led directly to a 2017 analysis that documents CEQA’s central role in the state’s decades-old shortage of housing, massively driving up the cost of all types of shelter and impoverishing millions of residents.

Yes, of course, some CEQA lawsuits are defensible and necessary.
But when you see the range of organizations that have vowed support for Proposition 45 — a modest CEQA reform on the November ballot sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce — it’s eye-opening.
The California Hospital Association, the California Farm Bureau, the California Senior Alliance and more than a half-dozen clean energy groups are among a vast list of institutions seeking relief from the migraines they face because of the broadly written, vague law.
Prop. 45 would impose a 365-day limit on official environmental reviews for projects ranging from broadband construction to building roads, homes and schools to wildfire mitigation. Courts would be given a maximum of 270 days to rule on CEQA suits after they are filed.
Contrary to claims that the changes would gut “the state’s strongest-in-the-nation environmental laws,” local governments would still have considerable authority in the approval process. Activists wouldn’t be muzzled.
This is reflected in the analysis of Prop. 45 from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
The LAO’s biggest concern had to do with potentially substantial implementation costs for state and local governments, not weakened green regulations. And the analysis also noted the benefit to governments of new revenue from ventures no longer blocked by CEQA — and from having their own projects cost less.
Prop. 45 won’t transform the state’s regulatory maze overnight. But it would make California’s planning approval process fairer, less expensive and considerably more predictable.
Yes on 45.

What Is Prop 45?
Proposition 45 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm), the Building an Affordable California Act (https://yesonprop45.com/read-the-measure/), is a 2026 California ballot proposition that modernizes the state's outdated approval process for essential projects like housing, water, clean energy, roads, schools and hospitals by setting enforceable timelines (https://yesonprop45.com/get-the-facts/) for agency decisions and court challenges, while keeping California's environmental, worker and tribal protections and local control (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) in place.

Prop 45 will:
Reduce the cost of living
An analysis by the Blue Sky Consulting Group estimates Prop 45 would add nearly 20,000 homes a year (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/), or nearly 200,000 over ten years.
Accelerate the essential infrastructure California needs
Agencies must approve or deny project applications within 365 days (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026), and courts must resolve legal challenges within 270 days (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/45/analysis.htm).
Protect taxpayers by keeping public projects on time and on budget
The same analysis estimates $386 million a year in savings for public agencies (https://yesonprop45.com/report-2026-09-25-economic-and-fiscal-impacts-of-proposition-45/) on essential projects and $250 million a year for California ratepayers.
Create good-paying jobs and strengthen our economy
Projects built under Prop 45 must meet California's strongest-in-the-nation labor standards (https://yesonprop45.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Prop-45-Labor-Protections-Fact-Sheet-8.19.26.pdf), including fair pay and safe job sites.
Protect local control and community input
Local governments keep full authority (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45) to approve, deny or condition projects, and Prop 45 guarantees a 45-day public comment period with written responses to all timely comments.
Protect California's strong environmental, worker and tribal cultural protections
Prop 45 does not weaken or eliminate any environmental law (https://www.hansonbridgett.com/publications/260730_2100_hb-letter-prop-45); CEQA (https://oag.ca.gov/environment/ceqa) remains fully in place.
Prop 45 speeds up approvals for the projects Californians rely on most:

Roads, bridges, transit and other transportation infrastructure
Wildfire prevention and resilience projects
Single and multi-family homes, senior and student housing
Clean energy generation, transmission and storage
Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure
Schools, classrooms and educational facilities

# No.

**Proposition 45 (November 3, 2026)** — the California Chamber of Commerce–sponsored initiative that would create an optional, expedited CEQA review track for projects it defines as "essential" (housing, water, clean energy, healthcare, transportation, broadband, schools, wildfire mitigation).

## Why I'd vote No, after weighing everything

**1. The right goal, the wrong vehicle.** CEQA genuinely needs reform — decades of NIMBY weaponization, union "greenmail," and decade-long lawsuits (e.g., UC Berkeley's People's Park, the 15-year Richardson Grove case) have made California unaffordable. But this is a 41-page rewrite of hyper-technical environmental law locked into statute that can only be amended by a two-thirds legislative vote. Even UC Davis law professor Chris Elmendorf, a leading CEQA expert, says "some of the changes are good and some may be bad, and who knows what second-order effects they will have."

**2. It's streamlining for sprawl, not just housing.** The measure fast-tracks freeway expansions and greenfield development with "ancillary infrastructure," lets the *applicant* develop the only project alternative, freezes environmental standards at the date of application, and was poll-tested to exclude high-speed rail and the Delta tunnel (the Yes campaign's own strategist admitted this). The NYT, Sierra Club, and even pro-density groups like SPUR flagged this as subsidizing exactly the car-dependent, fire-zone fringe growth CEQA was written to stop. Notably, many longtime CEQA reformers — Tom Steyer, SPUR, Gov. Newsom — declined to endorse it.

**3. Real accountability rollbacks, not just deadlines.** It caps public comment at 45 days and excludes late comments from the court record, narrows tribal consultation to only federally recognized tribes, prevents courts from halting whole projects (only non-compliant portions), allows just one round of litigation, and instructs judges to give "the fullest possible weight" to approving projects. And it's ambiguous on whether data centers qualify — likely to spawn the very litigation it claims to curb.

**4. The fiscal math is shaky.** The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst estimates initial costs for state/local governments in the high tens of millions, potentially exceeding $100 million annually, with uncertain long-term effects. The rosy "$75,000 savings per home" figures come from a study the campaign itself commissioned. Funding is dominated by utilities, developers, tech billionaires, and oil money (California Resources Corp gave $1M+).

**The honest counterargument:** The San Diego U-T, Sacramento Bee, Mercury News, OC Register, and ~28 other papers endorse it, backed by children's hospitals, the NAACP, LULAC, and affordable-housing builders — arguing the Legislature has dithered for 50 years and enforceable deadlines are overdue. That case is real. But Sacramento has now passed major CEQA reforms in 2024–2025 (including exempting most infill housing), and this measure's worst provisions — sprawl fast-tracking, frozen standards, weakened tribal and public input — fall hardest on exactly the projects CEQA exists to scrutinize, while its benefits accrue to its corporate funders.

**Bottom line: No.**
